title: LETTER 2: Letter to Editor — Financial Literacy in Rural India

blocks.content: Topic: Write a letter to the Editor of a national newspaper highlighting the importance of financial literacy in rural India and suggesting measures to improve it.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Financial literacy in rural areas is essential for expanding formal banking access and reducing reliance on unregulated moneylenders.
A formal Letter to the Editor must adhere to a standardized layout including Sender Address, Date, Receiver Address, Subject, Salutation, Body, and Subscription.
The body of the letter should clearly outline the problem, discuss its impact on rural communities, and propose actionable solutions like digital literacy drives.
Mentioning key government frameworks such as Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) strengthens the argument in competitive exam writing.

blocks.content: Promoting financial literacy in rural India is not merely an economic imperative, but a fundamental step towards inclusive national development.
Subject: Urgent Need to Promote Financial Literacy in Rural India

rows: Minimal paperwork with high collateral risk
Protected by banking ombudsman and laws
No regulatory oversight or legal recourse

blocks.content: Through the esteemed columns of your newspaper, I wish to draw the attention of the Government, banking institutions, and civil society to the urgent need for improving financial literacy in rural India. Despite commendable schemes like the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY), which has opened over 54 crore accounts, a significant proportion of rural account holders remain unaware of basic financial concepts such as interest rates, insurance, pension, or the dangers of predatory lending.

The consequences of financial illiteracy are deeply troubling. Farmers continue to borrow from moneylenders at exploitative rates of 24–60% per annum, unaware that the Kisan Credit Card offers credit at an effective rate of just 4%. Rural women, despite being the primary borrowers in Self Help Groups, frequently lack the knowledge to compare loan products or file grievances. The growing prevalence of financial fraud through unauthorised mobile apps and social media schemes further underscores this vulnerability.

I humbly urge the Reserve Bank of India, NABARD, and commercial banks to deploy trained financial literacy officers at the Gram Panchayat level, integrate financial education into school curricula from Class 6 onwards, and leverage Krishi Vigyan Kendras and Common Service Centres as financial literacy hubs. Regular melas, street plays, and vernacular language materials can make financial education culturally accessible.

An economically aware rural citizenry will not only protect itself from exploitation but will also drive the next wave of sustainable financial inclusion. I appeal to your publication to take up this cause and support awareness campaigns.

items: Never write personal names or actual addresses in the exam paper unless explicitly provided in the prompt; use 'XYZ' or 'Examination Hall'.
The subject line must be brief, precise, and placed directly between the Receiver's Address and the Salutation.
Do not ask the Editor to solve the problem directly; request them to publish the issue to draw the attention of relevant authorities.

blocks.content: Examiner's Tip: Letters to the Editor should have a hook sentence in the first paragraph. Use data (54 crore accounts, 4% interest) to show depth. The letter should end with a clear 'call to action'. Word count: approximately 280 words — ideal.
